title: Establishment of the Oval Office National Monument
Direct Sale of Public Land for Affordable Housing Purposes in Clark County, Nevada
summary: The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) proposes to sell a 10-acre parcel of public land located in Clark County, Nevada, under the authority of section 203 of the Federal Land Policy and Management Act of 1976, as amended (FLPMA); applicable BLM land sale regulations; and the Southern Nevada Public Land Management Act of 1998, as amended (SNPLMA). The BLM intends to conduct a direct sale of the parcel to Clark County, a political subdivision of the State of Nevada, at less than the appraised fair market value, for affordable housing purposes, consistent with the SNPLMA and applicable BLM policy.

title: Standard Instrument Approach Procedures, and Takeoff Minimums and Obstacle Departure Procedures; Miscellaneous Amendments
summary: This rule amends, suspends, or removes Standard Instrument Approach Procedures (SIAPs) and associated Takeoff Minimums and Obstacle Departure Procedures for operations at certain airports. These regulatory actions are needed because of the adoption of new or revised criteria, or because of changes occurring in the National Airspace System, such as the commissioning of new navigational facilities, adding new obstacles, or changing air traffic requirements. These changes are designed to provide for the safe and efficient use of the navigable airspace and to promote safe flight operations under instrument flight rules at the affected airports.

title: Respirable Crystalline Silica and Respiratory Protection
summary: This proposed rule clarifies and modifies provisions of the respirable crystalline silica and respiratory protection standards that were established in MSHA's 2024 final rule titled "Lowering Miners' Exposure to Respirable Crystalline Silica and Improving Respiratory Protection." The changes provide clarity and make improvements to the requirements for methods of compliance, exposure monitoring, respiratory protection, medical surveillance, and recordkeeping while maintaining strong protection of miners. title: National Television Multiple Ownership Rule
summary: In this document, the Federal Communications Commission (Commission) repeals the national television multiple ownership rule (national cap), which prohibits a commercial television licensee from having a cognizable interest in television stations that have an aggregate national audience reach above 39%. The Commission finds, given seismic changes in the modern media marketplace, that the rule's repeal will help empower local broadcast television stations to operate in the public interest and to better serve the needs and interests of their local communities. The Commission will review on a case-by-case basis proposed transactions that would have been prohibited under the national cap to determine whether a proposed transaction would serve the Commission's media ownership goals of localism, competition, and viewpoint diversity.

title: Rangeland Management
summary: The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA or Department) proposes to amend the regulations governing grazing and livestock use on the National Forest System to modernize grazing administration, improve clarity, codify existing policy, and expand opportunities for stewardship and access. The proposed amendments would update permit issuance, eligibility, and qualification provisions; establish a framework for adaptive response to drought, wildfire, and similar disturbance events; and expand authorities for stewardship-oriented livestock use, including adding the ability to implement stewardship projects (such as outcome-based grazing or targeted grazing) under a temporary grazing permit or livestock use permit. The proposed rule would revise grazing fee provisions to ensure consistent fee-setting across the national forests in the 16 contiguous Western States and the national grasslands, and establish a surcharge for authorized leasing of livestock by permittees. It would consolidate and renumber existing sections in subpart A for clarity and make conforming, technical, and administrative updates throughout part 222. The Department invites public comment on all aspects of the proposed rule.

title: National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence (NCCoE) Projects and Activities
summary: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence (NCCoE) invites organizations to submit letters of interest to participate in NCCoE collaborative research projects through a standing consortia structure. This Federal Register Notice (FRN) notifies interested parties that NIST is establishing a single process through which organizations may express interest in participating in one or more NCCoE project consortia. Rather than issuing a separate FRN for each new NCCoE project, NIST is posting a single partnership announcement in the Federal Register and directing interested parties to SAM.gov for further information. New NCCoE collaborative research projects will be announced on SAM.gov. Additionally, NIST will maintain a publicly available list of active and forming NCCoE projects on the NCCoE website (https://www.nccoe.nist.gov/portfolio), where instructions for letters of interest will also be posted. Organizations may submit letters of interest to participate in one or more consortia on a rolling basis. Selected participants will collaborate with NIST through Cooperative Research and Development Agreements (CRADAs), and contribute technology, expertise, and products to NCCoE cybersecurity demonstrations. Interested organizations should describe the technical expertise, services, and/or products that they will bring to NCCoE to support the Center's collaborative research activities. Participation is open to all interested organizations that can contribute their expertise, services, and/or products to the NCCoE's projects and activities. Selected participants will be required to enter into a CRADA with NIST. At NIST's discretion, entities that are not legally permitted to enter into CRADAs may be allowed to participate under a separate non-CRADA agreement.

title: Housing and Community Development Act of 1980: Verification of Eligible Status
summary: This final rule revises HUD's Section 214 regulations to require the verification of U.S. citizenship or the eligible immigration status of all applicants and recipients of assistance under a covered program regardless of age. The rule will also make prorated assistance a temporary condition pending verification of eligible status of all family members, where permitted by statute, as opposed to under HUD's current regulations where prorated assistance could continue indefinitely. These amendments bring HUD's regulations into greater alignment with the wording and purpose of Section 214 and align with the current Administration's priorities and regulatory reform efforts.

title: FY27 Social Impact Partnerships To Pay for Results Act Notice of Funding Opportunity
summary: Provide an evaluation design plan summary by following the following guidelines. Limit this to 3 pages or fewer. The summary should provide information demonstrating that the proposed evaluation will be designed to determine whether the outcomes were achieved as a result of the intervention. The summary must address the following six topics: i. Outcome metrics and data sources. Identify the outcome metric or metrics that will be used to determine whether the project achieved its outcome goals. For each metric, identify the data source, data owner, expected outcome target or payment threshold, and why the metric is an independent, objective indicator of impact that is not subject to manipulation by the service provider, intermediary, investors, or other project partners. ii. Evaluation design and comparison group. Identify the proposed evaluation design, such as a randomized controlled trial, regression discontinuity design, difference-in-differences design, matched comparison design, or another rigorous methodology. Describe the treatment group, the control or comparison group, how each group will be formed, and the expected difference in services received by each group. Briefly explain how the design will support causal conclusions. iii. Randomization feasibility. State whether random assignment is feasible. If random assignment is feasible, briefly describe how it would occur. If random assignment is not feasible, explain why and identify the strongest feasible alternative evaluation method. iv. Preliminary power calculation. Provide a preliminary power calculation for each primary outcome or payment metric. Identify the expected treatment and control or comparison group sizes, the expected effect the intervention is designed to achieve, and whether the proposed sample is large enough to detect that effect. Briefly state the main assumptions that affect the calculation, such as attrition, missing data, take-up, clustering, or repeated observations. v. Data access. Identify the data needed to conduct the evaluation, including data needed to measure outcomes, construct the treatment and control or comparison groups, and assess baseline characteristics. State the status of access to each major data source, including whether data-use agreements, memoranda of understanding, consent forms, or other approvals are in place or will be needed. If federal administrative data are required, identify the federal data source, expected access pathway, and any known gaps or risks. vi. Main risks to the evaluation. Identify the most important risks to the evaluation's ability to produce credible causal estimates, such as insufficient sample size, missing data, attrition, weak service contrast, contamination, changes in policy or service availability, implementation challenges, or inability to access required data. Briefly describe how the Applicant and independent evaluator expect to mitigate these risks. At the application stage, Applicants are not required to provide final regression equations, final covariate specifications, minimum detectable impact estimates, final hypothesis testing procedures, or a full implementation evaluation protocol. If selected for an award, the Awardee must submit a full Evaluation Design Plan after award, in the form and timeline required by Treasury. See Appendix III for a description of what will be required in the final evaluation design plan. (5) Independent evaluator qualifications: Provide a summary explaining the independence of the evaluator from the other entities involved in the project and the evaluator's experience in conducting rigorous evaluations of program effectiveness including, where available, well-implemented RCTs and quasi-experimental analyses on the intervention or similar interventions. When discussing experience, please note both personnel and organization experience. Applicants must address the following qualifications of the evaluator. Please limit this to 3 pages or fewer. i. Experience working with the datasets the project expects to use; ii. Prior work in conducting implementation and causal impact evaluation and how their past methodologies and evaluation design experience will be used in the proposed project. Please provide examples of evaluations that they have completed of similar size, scope and complexity; iii. Qualifications of the key personnel designing and overseeing the evaluation and ensuring its quality, including their education or training and type and years of experience; iv. Experience in managing similar evaluation protocols (e.g., type of sampling, data collection, analysis); and v. Experience dealing with unforeseen data or implementation issues in other program evaluations. Provide specific examples and experiences dealing with unforeseen data or implementation issues. (6) Independent evaluator contract or agreement. Provide a copy of the contract or agreement to be entered into between the State or local government and the independent evaluator. The contract or agreement must address the following information. i. Plan to obtain relevant datasets from various sources, for example, local agencies, state agencies, or other federal agencies, including the responsibilities of the grantee and evaluator in accomplishing this task; ii. Design and coding of a management information system, as needed, that is tailored for research or evaluation, to track participants and/or to obtain individual level data; iii. Collection or assessment of individual-level data. The independent evaluator must work directly with the Applicant and other organizations to enter into one or more agreements for the access and use of the data. These agreements must include assuring data quality and adherence to all federal and state data privacy statutes and policies and to all applicable data security standards; iv. Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval or a plan to get IRB approval to ensure the protection of human subjects, to the extent applicable; and v. Submission of progress reports to Treasury, the Interagency Council, and the head of the relevant agency in accordance with the reporting requirements described in Section 8.B.b, Evaluation Progress Reports and Section 8.B.c, Evaluation Final Report. vi. A payment plan that details the annual payment schedule that aligns with the other requirements of the independent evaluator. The selection of an independent evaluator is subject to the procurement requirements of the Uniform Guidance, including those related to competitive procurement.\11\ ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

title: Inspection Programs for Single-Engine Turbine-Powered Airplanes and Unmanned Aircraft; and Miscellaneous Maintenance-Related Updates
summary: The final rule updates the maintenance inspection requirements for single-engine turbine-powered airplanes and unmanned aircraft. Aircraft owners and operators now have more inspection program options to choose from and more relaxed mechanical reliability reporting requirements. It also clarifies various maintenance-related regulations. This final rule relieves aircraft owners, operators, maintenance providers, and FAA of certain workload burdens by facilitating a more efficient workload for these individuals without compromising aviation safety.

title: Modification to Work Requirements for Able-Bodied Adults
summary: The proposed rule would codify USDA's regulatory implementation of provisions of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025 (OBBB) changing the three-month time limit for certain participants subject to work requirements in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). These changes include modifying the list of exceptions from the time limit for certain populations; updating requirements for areas to qualify for waivers of the time limit; and adding the temporary good faith exemptions in Alaska and Hawaii. Additionally, this rule proposes to strengthen requirements for requesting waivers of the time limit and revise the SNAP definition of a homeless individual.

title: Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program: Reforming Categorical Eligibility
summary: Under section 5(a) of the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008, households in which each member receives benefits under a State program funded by Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) are categorically eligible for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). Current SNAP regulations consider TANF benefits to include both cash assistance and non-cash or in-kind benefits or services from TANF-funded programs. This proposal would limit categorical eligibility to only households that receive TANF assistance, as defined at 45 CFR 260.31. These revisions would ensure that SNAP benefits are targeted to needy households that have qualified for TANF assistance while still aligning categorical eligibility's statutory purpose of simplifying program administration. A 100-word summary of this rule has been posted to www.regulations.gov and can be found here.
